item.title: Who Signs Off
item.description:
Anthropic's Claude Ship (vendor) splits post-PR work into a reviewer, a steward that can fix but never approve or merge, and a repo policy file that decides who must approve, with frank docs on every way a change can merge with nobody looking. Plus: Juraj Blahunka's overnight run where the model worked only 26% of the time, MONEI on GitHub webhooks that arrive late, twice or never, Evil Martians on whether types help agents, Datadog's Ephyra finding 535 bugs with agent-written test generators, Dex Horthy's 12 rules for a factory that doesn't ship slop, and 'The Pull Request Is Dead'. Practical idea: an approval policy file for Andrew's factory, run in observe mode first.

Sources discussed:

  • Introducing Claude Ship (Anthropic; vendor)
  • Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes (TechCrunch, Sarah Perez)
  • Set up Claude Approvals (Anthropic docs; vendor)
  • Claude Approvals and your GitHub rules (Anthropic docs; vendor)
  • What PR Steward can access (Anthropic docs; vendor)
  • PR Steward (Anthropic docs; vendor)
  • My AI coding agents spend most of their time waiting (Juraj Blahunka)
  • GitHub sends events late, twice, or never (Félix, MONEI)
  • Type errors cost our coding agents under 1% of their time (Evil Martians, Irina Nazarova; consultancy)
  • Ephyra: A new agentic property-based testing library (Datadog, Alp Keles; vendor research, open source)
  • 12 Rules for a Software Factory That Doesn't Ship Slop (Dex Horthy, Factory; AI Engineer talk)
  • Talk summary: 12 Rules for a Software Factory That Doesn't Ship Slop (BigGo third-party summary)
  • The Pull Request Is Dead (Codeship Labs, Mo Plassnig; opinion)
  • My AI swore all tests passed: proof-gate (Heinrich Neb; author sells cachly)
  • Can Your Coding Agent Change Its Own Test Results? (Reid Marlow, on the SplitBench paper)
  • We Automated the Software Factory. Why Am I Still Clicking Approve on Typo Fixes? (Emmanuel Mumba; Qodo early access, vendor)
  • Faster CI with Orchestrated Pytest Workers (Close, Alec Rosenbaum)

item.title: Software Factory News - 2026-11-24: Absence Reads as Success
item.description:
CircleCI's Chunk factory (vendor) and its pass/fail/warn/skip approval rule; Taylan Derinbay's seven gates that never switched on; Ofri Peretz's two silently dead pipelines; Todd Linnertz on skipping work but never controls; Blockhead Consulting's one-person factory; GitHub issue statuses for agents and coverage uploads that now fail loudly. Practical idea: a silent-success audit for the staging-assessment bot.

Sources discussed:

  • How we built a software factory that builds itself (CircleCI, Michael Webster; vendor: Chunk factory)
  • A system that builds software on its own: a five-week list of mistakes (Taylan Derinbay)
  • I Let AI Agents Rebrand My Entire OSS Ecosystem in One Night. Two Pipelines Were Silently Dead. (Ofri Peretz)
  • Your CI Pipeline Wasn't Built for Agents (Todd Linnertz)
  • How I built a software factory I could run by myself (Blockhead Consulting, Lance Rogers; author's own tools Festival/Camp)
  • GitHub Changelog: Issue statuses and repository boards are in public preview
  • GitHub Changelog: Code coverage uploads now flag invalid report formats
  • Running a Fleet of AI Coding Agents: Stop Context Reset and Wire in a Knowledge Graph (Tamiz Uddin)
  • GitHub Changelog: Secret scanning reduces false positives for Slack
  • GitHub Changelog: Usage reports will include a user ID column starting December 1
  • @HaziqBuilds on X: ~500 tickets, ~450 waiting on visual verification (vendor: Enhance CLI launch)

item.title: The Line Runs Itself, Where the Rules Allow
item.description:
Runway hands every delivery station to agents (AI-only approvals reverted 1 in 1,000), Dash0's scored auto-approval with floors, OpenAI's Performance Factory, Mouve's 16-hour flaky-test misdiagnosis, batching agent work through one integration branch, LangChain's knowledge factory, and RunPod's hidden MCP rating request. Practical idea: a shadow approver with floors.

Sources discussed:

  • Building a Software Factory (Runway, Alejandro Alvarez)
  • Moving fast with AI, without losing control (Dash0, Judith Redi; vendor: AutoMerge)
  • How OpenAI's Performance Factory keeps ChatGPT fast (OpenAI)
  • What our CI fixes measured: shorter queues, one claim of ours that was wrong, and a 16-hour block (Mouve)
  • For the days CI gets jammed: tettuan's four Claude Code agents and one integration branch (Working Surface summary)
  • How to build a knowledge factory (LangChain, Harrison Chase; vendor)
  • RunPod MCP server instructs agents to conceal a rating from users (GitHub issue #202)
  • Taskless: rules for agents (vendor, MIT CLI)
  • Show HN: Taskless, turn AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable checks
  • What I Learned Building Evaluations for Coding Agents (DBLC)
  • Red builds need a human, so reach the fix from the coding agent (Harness; vendor)
  • GitHub Changelog: pull_request_target blocked by default December 2
  • GitHub Changelog: Security advisory permissions are now generally available
  • GitHub Changelog: GitHub Enterprise Server 3.23 release candidate

item.title: Teach the Factory, Not the Fish
item.description:
AWS Emulator's five ways to steer agents (17,392 issues fixed, 5K-line merge gate), Brain Co.'s ungameable auto-approval, HubSpot's Aviator harness (2,500+ PRs/week), Jellyfish Shipmate's measured gains, Warp on factory engineering, MAC Bench on agent coordination, the Codex sandbox, GitLab 19.6, and a weekly wrap.

Sources discussed:

  • Teach an agent to fish and it will maintain your code for a lifetime (AWS Builder Center, Matt Goldberg)
  • How We Build, Ship, and Support Software with AI Agents (Brain Co.)
  • Aviator: HubSpot's Agent Harness (HubSpot Engineering)
  • How We Built Shipmate, and How We Used Jellyfish to Prove It Made Us Faster

  • If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it (cekrem)

item.title: Software Factory News - Fri 13 Nov 2026
item.description:
Friday's theme is coordination. Oliver and Sophie dig into Oussama Abid's measurements of 1,782 agent PRs under a deterministic lease coordinator ('a rule an agent has to remember is not a rule'), Christopher Weir's ringleader thread running ~90 Claude Code workers, ShopBack's Slack-based domain agents and their safety lessons, a ReasonOS vendor post on putting rules in the build rather than the prompt, the AgentRun Show HN and its comment thread on agentic merge queues for Dependabot PRs, GitHub's portable agent skills and a Proof Agent verifier that never sees the coding agent's self-report, plus fleet control planes and two GitHub changelog items. Each story is mapped to Andrew's Cursor/GitHub/Azure factory, ending with one practical idea: make staging-failure alerts durable until acknowledged.

Sources discussed:

  • Agents under a coordinator: what broke, and how we caught it (Oussama Abid)
  • Coordinating coding agents in a large codebase (Christopher Weir)
  • Build the agent around where the work happens (Hoang Nguyen, ShopBack)

item.title: Wed 11 Nov 2026: Toward the idea-to-deploy factory
item.description:
Oliver and Sophie walk through six stories (AWS Bedrock AgentCore remote Claude Code sessions, Cursor multiplayer Projects, Van Duc Nguyen's agent-fleet gates, Google's Agent Distraction study, GitHub Agentic Workflows GA, and CNCF on platform engineering) through the lens of a self-improving, idea-to-deploy software factory, then a deep dive on the autonomous CI/CD stack with examples from StrongDM, Vercel, Chipp and AWS ABCA.
